title: Design an API Gateway with ASP.NET Core and gRPC
description: Use YARP or Ocelot as an API gateway and gRPC for efficient internal service communication.

data.text: You have 8 microservices. Clients need a single endpoint. Design an API gateway that routes, authenticates, and transforms requests.
An API Gateway sits between clients and services. It centralizes cross-cutting concerns like authentication, logging, rate limiting, and request transformation.

data.title: Gateway Responsibilities
items: **Routing**: Map public endpoints to internal services
**Authentication**: Validate JWT or cookies once at the edge
**Rate Limiting**: Protect downstream services from abuse
**Request/Response Transformation**: Translate between HTTP and gRPC

data.text: YARP (Yet Another Reverse Proxy) is Microsoft's production-ready reverse proxy for ASP.NET Core. It supports dynamic configuration, transforms, and load balancing.
gRPC uses HTTP/2 and Protocol Buffers. It is faster and more strongly typed than REST for internal service-to-service calls.

data.title: gRPC Service and Client

data.text: The gateway validates the JWT once. It then forwards claims to internal services via headers. Internal services trust the gateway and skip authentication.

data.title: JWT Validation at the Gateway
Gateway Pattern Trade-offs
data.text: A gateway centralizes cross-cutting concerns but adds latency and a single point of failure. Use clustering and health checks to make it resilient.

data.title: Key Takeaways
points: YARP is the recommended reverse proxy for ASP.NET Core
Gateways centralize auth, logging, and rate limiting
gRPC is more efficient than REST for internal service calls
Forward authenticated user info via headers to downstream services
Always make the gateway stateless so it can scale horizontally
data.takeaway: An API gateway simplifies client integration and protects internal services. Combine it with gRPC for efficient, strongly-typed internal communication.
